passage: Tushar here, one desk over. Ganga is the one who keeps our Monday stand-up light, usually with a joke about her own coffee habit. Last week a new colleague, Rohit, made a joke about another colleague's accent, and two people laughed. Ganga didn't. She noticed the colleague looking down at the table and said easily, "Let's skip the accent jokes, everyone here has one." Then she turned to the colleague: "How did the client call go?" The subject moved on. Later, in the corridor, Ganga told Rohit, "It didn't seem to land well with them. Better to keep the jokes about ourselves." Rohit said sorry to me, not to the colleague, which I found odd. I couldn't tell whether Ganga was angry or just tired.

qa.q: What did Ganga usually joke about at the stand-up?
qa.a: Her own coffee habit.

qa.q: What might Ganga have been feeling when she saw the colleague look down at the table?
qa.a: She probably felt concern for them, seeing the laughter had not included them, though Tushar cannot say whether she was angry or tired.

qa.q: Why did Ganga speak to Rohit privately later?
qa.a: It let her explain what did not land without embarrassing Rohit publicly, and suggest keeping humour about ourselves.

qa.q: How might the colleague whose accent was joked about have felt?
qa.a: Likely uncomfortable or embarrassed, as looking down at the table suggests; the laughter alone does not show they were fine with it.

grounding: A young professional uses light humour about herself and steps in when a joke about a colleague's identity makes someone look uncomfortable, seen by a peer.

passage:
Tuesday. In the team meeting Disha joked about Mehak's typo in the client deck: "Well, at least the client now knows we can't spell their name." Everyone laughed, Mehak too, though her smile was tight and she closed her laptop.
Thursday. Disha noticed Mehak had stopped chatting at lunch. She said, "I made that joke about your typo and I think it landed badly. I'm sorry. Did it?" Mehak took a moment. "A bit. I was already worried about it."
The following Wednesday. In the meeting Disha joked about her own late-night snacks, and Mehak laughed properly. Later Mehak said, "Thanks for asking."

qa.q: What did Disha joke about in the team meeting?
qa.a: Mehak's typo in the client deck.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she laughed with a tight smile?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and worried about her typo, though laughing along may also have been an effort to fit in.

qa.q: What did Disha do that repaired things?
qa.a: She noticed the change, apologised and asked directly, then moved to jokes about herself.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt on noticing Mehak had stopped chatting at lunch?
qa.a: Disha probably felt uneasy and a little guilty, sensing the typo joke had landed badly, which is why she apologised and asked.

grounding: A young professional learns that a joke about a colleague's mistake can hurt even when people laugh, apologises, and moves to humour about herself.

passage: Farida, the whole team laughed when Mohan joked about Priya's accent today, and Priya laughed too. Let me, Harish, tell you why that doesn't settle it. At twenty-four I was the office comedian at a bank branch in Nashik. There was a clerk, Suresh, who once misfiled a whole day's cheques. For months I called him "Cheque-mate" in every meeting. Everyone laughed, Suresh loudest of all. I thought we were friends. Then one evening I found him in the stairwell, head in his hands. He said, "Every time you say it, the manager looks at me like I'm the idiot again." I felt sick. His laugh had been armour. I apologised the next morning, in front of the same people, and I never used the name again. Jokes about the rain, about myself, about the canteen dal, fine. Never about someone's mistake, looks or where they come from. And watch the face, not the laugh.

qa.q: What nickname did Harish give Suresh?
qa.a: 'Cheque-mate'.

qa.q: How did Harish feel on finding Suresh in the stairwell?
qa.a: Harish felt sick with guilt, realising Suresh's laugh had been armour and the joke had hurt him.

qa.q: What choice did Harish make after that turning point?
qa.a: Harish apologised publicly the next morning in front of the same people and stopped using the nickname, keeping jokes to harmless topics.

qa.q: How had Suresh experienced the nickname?
qa.a: Suresh felt humiliated, feeling the manager saw him as an idiot each time, though he laughed loudest to hide it.

grounding: An elder recalls a running joke about a colleague's mistake, learning that laughter did not mean consent, and apologising.

passage: Elizabeth had the microphone at the team offsite in Goa, with thirty people, a sound system that squealed, and five minutes to fill before dinner. Her notes had a roast-style bit about the quarter: the server crash, the flooded office, and Anjali's spreadsheet that had emailed the whole client list to the wrong group. It would get a big laugh. She glanced at Anjali in the second row. Anjali's shoulders were already up, her smile fixed; people had teased her about the email for weeks. Elizabeth skipped the line and joked about her own disastrous attempt to book the bus instead, and the room laughed. Then someone at the back called out, "Tell the spreadsheet story!" A few people laughed. Elizabeth kept her voice light but clear. "Nope. That one's retired. Anjali's fixed more than any of us this year." People clapped. Later, at the buffet, Anjali squeezed her arm. "Thank you. I was dreading that."

qa.q: How many people were at the offsite?
qa.a: Thirty people.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as Elizabeth took the microphone?
qa.a: Anjali was likely tense and dreading being teased again about the email, with raised shoulders and a fixed smile.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth handle humour boundaries under pressure?
qa.a: She dropped the joke about Anjali's mistake, joked about herself instead, and when someone called for the story, lightly but clearly refused and praised Anjali.

qa.q: What would have happened if Elizabeth had told the spreadsheet story?
qa.a: The room might have laughed loudly, but Anjali would likely have felt humiliated again, with the laughter hiding her discomfort.

grounding: Shows a young professional using light humour to build rapport while refusing a joke about a colleague's mistake when she looks uncomfortable.

passage: At the Friday lunch in the Bengaluru office, Raghav was on a roll. He'd already done a good bit about the lift that stopped at every floor, and Noor had laughed as hard as anyone. Then he turned to Tenzin, who had joined from Darjeeling two weeks ago, and made a joke about his face and where he "really" came from. A few people laughed. Tenzin laughed too, a short sound, then looked down at his plate and didn't look up again. Noor saw it. Laughter, she thought, isn't the same as being okay. She didn't want to shame Raghav in front of everyone, but she didn't want to let it pass either. "Raghav, the lift material was better," she said lightly, and changed the subject. After lunch she caught him alone. "That joke about Tenzin landed badly. Did you see his face?" Raghav frowned, then nodded. "I'll talk to him." Noor messaged Tenzin: "That wasn't okay. Want to grab chai?"

qa.q: Where did Tenzin join from?
qa.a: From Darjeeling.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have been feeling after the joke?
qa.a: Tenzin likely felt hurt and uncomfortable, laughing briefly to get through it and then looking down at his plate.

qa.q: How did Noor respond to the joke?
qa.a: She redirected lightly in the moment, then spoke to Raghav privately about Tenzin's reaction, and checked in with Tenzin with an offer of chai.

qa.q: How did Raghav react when Noor spoke to him privately?
qa.a: Raghav frowned, then accepted it and said he would talk to Tenzin.

grounding: Shows a young professional noticing that a colleague's laugh at a joke about his identity hid discomfort, and responding to it.

passage:
At the Friday team lunch, one of the sales team held up Ritu's new ID photo on his phone. "Ritu's new look! Very... mushroom." The table laughed. Ritu laughed too, a short sound, and pulled her dupatta closer.
Divyansh didn't laugh. "Nah, that one's not fair. The ID camera makes everyone look like a suspect. Mine looks like I've just been arrested."
He held up his own. The table laughed harder, at him this time, and the phone went down.
Later, near the lift, Ritu said quietly, "Thanks. I laughed because what else do you do."
"I know. That's why I said something. Laughing along doesn't mean it's okay with you."
"Some days I don't mind jokes. Just not about how I look."
"Noted. I'll stick to bad ID photos of myself and the office coffee."
She smiled properly this time. "Deal."

qa.q: What did the sales colleague call Ritu's new look?
qa.a: He called it "Very... mushroom."

qa.q: What did Ritu's short laugh and pulling her dupatta closer suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Ritu felt uncomfortable and self-conscious, laughing only because she didn't know what else to do.

qa.q: How did Divyansh shift the joke without starting a fight?
qa.a: He said it wasn't fair, then turned the humour on his own ID photo, so the table laughed at him and the phone went down.

qa.q: How did the rest of the table seem to read Ritu's laugh?
qa.a: They seemed to take it as her being fine with the joke, since she laughed too, missing the signs of discomfort.

grounding: A young professional avoids jokes about a colleague's appearance and responds when she looks uncomfortable, since laughing along does not prove she is okay with it.
